newsitem.title: UK: Tanker rates to rise in 1997, may dip later - SSY.
newsitem.headline: Tanker rates to rise in 1997, may dip later - SSY.

text.p: Dirty and clean tanker rates are likely to rise further this year despite a fairly large number of newbuildings, brokers Simpson Spence and Young (SSY) said on Wednesday.
But they said in their Annual Shipping Outlook that the longer-term outlook was less rosy unless there is marked increase in tanker demolitions.

"Despite quite a high volume of tanker newbuildings awaiting delivery before 1998, freight rates look set to strengthen further in 1997 -- especially as much of this year's projected rise in oil use is in areas that are heavily dependent on imports," the report said.

"Prospective growth of product demand and crude supply should bring a new peak in seaborne oil trade, albeit that high crude supplies in the Atlantic Basin will again mean limited expansion of tonne-mile employment, especially on the AG Mideast Gulf -West route," it added.
"Owners can take some consolation, though, that widespread crude availability outside the Middle East allows increased back-haul trading opportunities, even for VLCCs very large crude carriers.

"Furthermore, this abundance of short-haul crude should be partly offset by the growth of 'balancing trades' to redress regional shortages of respective cargo grades in some regions (e.g. light, sweet crude in Asia)."

SSY said new refining capacity in Asia implied a further large increase in eastbound VLCC shipments and added, "the greater tendency for Korean charterers to fix modern units means that Japanese interests will face greater competition for such ships than previously, which could translate into higher premiums for newer tonnage on these routes."

SSY said the clean (refined product) tanker market would benefit from increased U.S. imports as refineries there were already operating virtually at capacity, while Asian trade would grow due to population increases, rises in car ownership, greater air travel and further expansion of the petrochemical industry.

"At present, the trading outlook for tankers appears more positive than for many years, with growth of seaborne trade volumes and the increasing importance accorded to vessel quality justifying greater optimism among owners," the report said.
It added: "However, tonnage supply developments look set to stall the current upturn before 1999.

"While the volume of new tonnage due to enter service this year is the lowest since 1990, in the past 12 months the tanker order-book, which had fallen by 10.5 Mdwt million deadweight tonnes, has been growing again (up by 3.9 Mdwt last year).
"Moreover, some of the new ships contracted do not yet have secure employment -- the first case in recent years of speculative tanker orders being placed.

"Unless there is a noteworthy increase in oil carrier demolition to offset this, progress towards more balanced markets would be arrested, and prospects for further firming of rates beyond 1997 correspondingly reduced."
"Even the need to comply with double-hull legislation shows no sign to date of inducing greater scrapping, making restraint in newbuilding ordering even more imperative," SSY said.
